The two-car Green Line train was traveling outbound near Kenmore Station around 3:15 p.m. when it rear-ended a stationary train stopped at a red signal, according to the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA).

"We were moving pretty fast, and suddenly there was no slowing down—just a massive boom," Jenkins told CNN affiliate WHDH. "It felt like an explosion. People were screaming, phones went flying everywhere, and the front of the car just buckled. It was total chaos."

"Our residents and visitors deserve to know that when they step onto public transit, their safety is the top priority," Wu said in a statement. "To learn that this occurred because someone was on their phone is infuriating. We demand full accountability."

**By Sarah Jenkins and Marcus Vance**
*The Boston Chronicle*

**BOSTON** — A violent Green Line collision that injured nearly 50 passengers and caused millions of dollars in damage was directly caused by a trolley operator who was distracted by texting on his personal cell phone, federal safety officials confirmed in a damning report released Thursday.

The crash occurred during the Friday evening commute near Government Center Station when a two-car trolley rammed into the rear of a stationary train at approximately 10 mph. Emergency responders rushed to the subterranean station shortly after 5:45 p.m. as frantic passengers poured out of the tunnel onto street level. Photographers captured scenes of bloodied commuters being loaded into ambulances on stretchers, while others leaned against concrete barriers, visibly shaken.

Passengers inside the trailing train described a scene of sudden horror as the collision threw people from their seats and shattered overhead glass.

"We were rolling along normally, and then there was this deafening crunch," said Arthur Pendelton, 38, of Brookline, who was riding in the front car of the impacting train. "People flew forward like ragdolls. The air filled with dust and smoke, and everyone was screaming. It was pure chaos. To find out he was just texting... it makes me furious."

The Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) immediately terminated the operator, who now faces criminal charges of gross negligence and reckless endangerment. Authorities have withheld his name pending formal arraignment.

The incident has sent shockwaves through the transit agency, exposing glaring loopholes in the enforceability of existing driver distraction rules. While the MBTA previously discouraged personal phone use, enforcement relied largely on self-reporting and spot checks.

Speaking at a news conference outside the MBTA headquarters, MBTA General Manager Daniel Grabauskas offered a stark apology to the victims and announced a sweeping, immediate policy shift.

"Effective immediately, the MBTA is implementing a strict, zero-tolerance ban on all personal electronic devices. If an operator is caught with a cell phone in the cab—on or off, texting or not—they will be terminated on the spot. No warnings. No second chances."

The impact buckled the steel framing, shattered glass, and threw passengers from their seats. Emergency crews descended into the subterranean darkness, ultimately transporting 46 passengers and crew members to local hospitals with injuries ranging from severe whiplash and lacerations to fractured bones.

Initial speculation questioned whether the Green Line’s notoriously aging infrastructure or a faulty braking system was to blame. However, NTSB field investigators quickly focused on the lead operator’s actions inside the cab.

Under questioning by federal and state authorities, Welch made a stunning admission: he had been texting his girlfriend on his personal cell phone just seconds before the impact.

Subpoenaed phone records corroborated the confession, showing an outbound text message transmitted precisely at the time of the crash. Welch admitted to investigators that he was typing the message with one hand while operating the multi-ton passenger vehicle with the other. Distracted by the screen, he completely missed a restrictive signal—a red light—and failed to see the taillights of the stationary trolley ahead until it was too late to deploy the emergency brakes.

"This wasn't a tragic accident born of equipment failure," said one lead NTSB investigator during a briefing. "This was a completely avoidable disaster caused by a total lapse in professional responsibility."

"If you are operating an MBTA vehicle, your hands belong on the controls, and your eyes belong on the tracks. Period. If you break this rule, you will no longer work for this agency."

In addition to the device ban, the MBTA announced plans to accelerate safety audits and explore automatic train protection (ATP) upgrades that would electronically stop a Green Line trolley if it overruns a red signal, removing human error from the safety equation.

Transit advocacy groups welcomed the swift policy shift but stressed that cultural changes within the agency must accompany strict rules.

"Passengers trust the MBTA with their lives every day," said a spokesperson for a local transit watchdog group. "A zero-tolerance rule on cell phones is the absolute baseline for ensuring that a preventable disaster like the Park-to-Government Center crash never happens again."
